content.title: What are Wrapper Classes?
content.description: Wrapper classes are object representations of Java's primitive data types. They allow primitive values to be treated as objects, making them compatible with collections, generics, and utility methods.

content.content: Java provides wrapper classes for every primitive data type. These classes belong to the java.lang package and enable developers to use primitive values wherever objects are required. Wrapper classes also provide useful methods for parsing, converting, and comparing values.

content.title: Why Wrapper Classes?
content.content: Collections like ArrayList can only store objects, not primitive data types. Wrapper classes bridge this gap.
Primitive Types and Their Wrapper Classes
Each primitive data type has a corresponding wrapper class with additional methods for conversions and utility operations.

content.title: Wrapper Classes in Java
content.description: The eight wrapper classes are Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, and Boolean.

content.content: Wrapper objects can be created using constructors (deprecated in many cases) or by using utility methods such as valueOf().

content.title: Creating Wrapper Objects

content.content: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of a primitive value into its corresponding wrapper object. Java performs this conversion automatically when required.

content.title: Autoboxing Example
Did You Know?
content.content: Autoboxing was introduced in Java 5 to simplify working with wrapper classes.
Unboxing is the automatic conversion of a wrapper object back into its primitive value.

content.title: Unboxing Example

content.content: Wrapper classes provide several built-in methods for converting strings, comparing values, and finding limits of data types.
Java Collections Framework stores objects instead of primitive data types. Wrapper classes make it possible to store numeric and boolean values inside collections like ArrayList.

content.title: Wrapper Class with ArrayList
Gift Wrapping
content.content: A primitive value is like a simple gift item. A wrapper class is like wrapping that gift inside a decorative box so it can be safely transported, stored, and handled in different situations.

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Questions about wrapper classes, autoboxing, unboxing, parseInt(), valueOf(), and the difference between primitive and wrapper types are very common in Java interviews.

items.question: Why can't ArrayList<int> be used?
items.answer: Because Java collections accept only objects, not primitive data types.

items.question: What happens if parseInt() receives an invalid number?
Why should wrapper objects be checked for null before unboxing?
items.answer: Unboxing a null wrapper object causes a NullPointerException.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: Use primitive types for performance and wrapper classes whenever objects are required, especially in collections and generics.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Every primitive type has a corresponding wrapper class.
Wrapper classes allow primitives to behave like objects.
Autoboxing converts primitives into wrapper objects automatically.
Unboxing converts wrapper objects back to primitives.
Wrapper classes provide useful conversion and utility methods.
